title: Nonlocality without entanglement for multipartite quantum measurements
abstract: We show that a pair of two-qubit product measurements can be perfectly distinguished when accessed jointly, yet cannot be perfectly distinguished when their local components are distributed between distant parties restricted to local quantum operations and classical communication (LOCC). This establishes a measurement analogue of nonlocality without entanglement that, unlike its state-based counterpart, emerges in a remarkably simple setting. We further uncover a hierarchy of LOCC discrimination strategies: adaptive protocols, in which the probe used at one site may depend on classical information obtained from another, can strictly outperform restricted non-adaptive protocols, as demonstrated by a set of six bipartite qutrit product measurements. We also show that LOCC distinguishability of bipartite measurements can be intrinsically directional, depending on which party initiates the protocol. More generally, we construct pairs of $n$-qubit product measurements that are globally perfectly distinguishable but cannot be perfectly distinguished across any bipartition, even when all parties on either side of the bipartition are allowed arbitrary joint quantum operations. Finally, we show how quantum data hiding based on quantum-process nonlocality without entanglement can be realized using elementary optical components.
summary: This work explores nonlocality in quantum measurements, demonstrating a measurement analogue of NLWE that is simpler than its state-based counterpart. The authors prove that certain multipartite measurements are globally distinguishable but cannot be distinguished by local operations and classical communication (LOCC). This has implications for quantum data hiding and the fundamental limits of local quantum processing.
main_problem: The paper investigates the concept of 'Nonlocality Without Entanglement' (NLWE) applied to quantum measurements, contrasting it with the well-known state-based phenomenon.
main_result: It establishes a measurement analogue of NLWE, showing that certain product measurements are globally distinguishable but cannot be perfectly distinguished using only Local Operations and Classical Communication (LOCC) across any bipartition.
method: The analysis uses formal definitions of measurement distinguishability, comparing global distinguishability (GD) against LOCC distinguishability (LDR/LDA) using fidelity and reduced state analysis.
model_or_system: The model involves multipartite quantum measurements, specifically pairs of two-qubit or general $n$-qubit product measurements, analyzed using quantum information theory tools.
key_observables: Success probability of distinguishing measurements, fidelity ($F$), and the distinguishability gap between GD and LOCC protocols.
important_parameters: The number of qubits ($n$), the type of measurement (product measurements), and the communication constraints (LOCC vs. joint operations).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to probe the measurements using specific entangled probe states and relies on the properties of fidelity (multiplicativity and monotonicity).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate circuit diagrams detailing protocols for distinguishing bipartite product measurements under GD, LDR, and LDA strategies.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the measurement analogue of NLWE using simple product measurements, then developing a hierarchy of local discrimination strategies (LDR vs. LDA), and finally generalizing the result to arbitrary $n$-qubit measurements.
why_interesting: The findings provide a fundamental resource theory perspective on quantum correlations, showing that nonlocality can be encoded in the measurement process itself, which has implications for quantum cryptography and device-independent protocols.
